results.summary_before: This is a basic Pong game implemented in Chisel that outputs a VGA video signal with two-bit-per-channel color and separate horizontal and vertical sync. Four input pins control the two paddles, and two more enable autopilot for either player, while bidirectional pins expose game state, sync signals, loss indicators, and a game tick. The documentation is minimal, describing it only as a Chisel template, and testing currently uses cocotb with a planned move to ChiselTest. No external hardware beyond a VGA display and buttons is described, and no silicon results are reported.

It requires an external SPI SRAM and an external VGA breakout board to operate. The documentation is minimal and does not explain how the computer works or how to test it. The design is notable for being created under extreme time pressure, but its functionality is uncertain.

It is intended to be used as a template for building more complex 7-segment projects. No specific inputs or outputs are documented beyond the display segments. The design is a starting point for beginners and was created at a Hackaday workshop.

results.summary_before: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray casting engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, rendering textured walls with flat-colored floor and ceiling while racing the beam. The player point of view is controlled via SPI, and an optional external QSPI memory can supply textures instead of internally generated ones. It outputs standard 640x480 VGA at 25.175 MHz and includes debug and demo modes, though the documentation notes that testing details are still to be confirmed. It is a resubmission of a previous Tiny Tapeout design and lacks doors, sprites, or other game elements.

results.summary_before: This design implements a stochastic multiplier, adder and self-multiplier using serial bit streams, with an LFSR-based stochastic number generator and a digital quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron as an application. Numbers are entered as two repeating 9-bit serial streams and results are read out serially on separate output pins. Testing requires an ADALM2000 to generate and capture the serial streams. The documentation is largely a reference list with images, so the exact internal architecture is only partly described.

results.summary_before: This is a 4-bit incrementer that takes a 4-bit input on ui[0:3] and produces a 5-bit output on uo[0:4], presumably the input plus one. The documentation says only to test it, without describing expected values or a test procedure. It requires VCC as external hardware according to the project notes. The design is a minimal Wokwi exercise with almost no useful documentation.
